findings.title: Manual unsigned int parsing without proper EOF handling
findings.impact: Incorrect EOF detection leading to silent data corruption or misaligned frame parsing. The method doesn't distinguish between a byte value of 0xFF and EOF condition.
findings.evidence: Lines 227-232: readUnsignedInt reads 4 individual bytes via in.read() and checks if ANY is negative (EOF). However, in.read() returning -1 is indistinguishable from the byte 0xFF without explicit EOF handling. The logic is correct but brittle.

findings.title: Unvalidated scale parameter in BigDecimal construction
findings.impact: Unexpected behavior or exceptions when parsing BigDecimal field values. A very large scale value (e.g., Integer.MAX_VALUE) could cause performance issues or precision loss.
findings.evidence: Lines 172-175: scale is read as unsigned byte and used directly without validation. A scale >= 128 is unusual for AMQP; no check ensures it is in reasonable bounds.

findings.title: Unbounded table field collection leading to memory exhaustion
findings.impact: DoS via crafted messages containing tables with thousands of field entries. No limit on field count; an attacker can create a pathological message with a valid tableLength but millions of tiny fields, exhausting memory and CPU.
findings.evidence: Lines 139-155: readTable() allocates a HashMap and loops reading fields without any limit on the number of entries added. If an attacker crafts a malicious frame with tableLength=1MB containing 100k tiny fields, the HashMap will grow unbounded.

findings.title: Unbounded memory allocation in readBytes from untrusted input
findings.impact: Denial of Service (DoS) attack via memory exhaustion. An attacker can craft a malicious AMQP message with a large content-length field, causing the parser to attempt allocating arrays up to 2GB, exhausting heap memory and crashing the JVM.
findings.evidence: Lines 86-90: contentLength is read as unsigned int (0 to 4GB), but only checked if it is less than Integer.MAX_VALUE. No upper bound validation or rate limiting. A contentLength of 2GB would be allocated on line 88: byte[] buffer = new byte[(int)contentLength].

findings.title: Unreliable stream EOF detection in readArray
findings.impact: Similar to F-002: infinite loops or incorrect parsing of array data due to unreliable available() detection.
findings.evidence: Lines 241-248: TruncatedInputStream is wrapped and readArray relies on available() > 0 to detect end-of-array, which is unreliable.

findings.title: Unbounded array element collection leading to memory exhaustion
findings.impact: DoS via crafted arrays with millions of elements, causing memory exhaustion and slow parsing.
findings.evidence: Lines 237-249: readArray() has no limit on array.size(). An attacker can create a frame with length=10MB containing millions of null entries, exhausting heap memory.

findings.title: Resource leak: TruncatedInputStream not explicitly closed
findings.impact: Potential resource leak if TruncatedInputStream holds file handles or other resources. While DataInputStream typically wraps in-memory streams, best practice is to close resources explicitly.
findings.evidence: Lines 146-147 and 241-242: TruncatedInputStream objects are created but never explicitly closed. If TruncatedInputStream opens underlying resources, they may not be released.

findings.title: Potential integer overflow in timestamp multiplication
findings.impact: Incorrect or wrapped timestamp values if in.readLong() returns a value near Long.MAX_VALUE. Multiplication by 1000 could overflow.
findings.evidence: Line 269: new Date(in.readLong()*1000) does not check for overflow. If in.readLong() > Long.MAX_VALUE/1000 (~9.2e15), multiplication overflows silently.

findings.title: Unreliable stream EOF detection using available() method
findings.impact: Infinite loops or incorrect parsing of table data. The available() method is unreliable and does not accurately report remaining bytes. Wrapping a DataInputStream with TruncatedInputStream may not properly signal EOF, causing the while loop to behave unpredictably.
findings.evidence: Lines 146-148: A TruncatedInputStream wrapper is created, but the code relies on available() > 0 to detect end-of-table. DataInputStream.available() is documented as unreliable and may return 0 even when bytes remain, or return non-zero when EOF is near.

findings.title: No maximum nesting depth for recursive table/array structures
findings.impact: Stack overflow via deeply nested table or array structures. An attacker can craft a message with tables containing tables containing tables (or arrays of arrays), causing unbounded recursion.
findings.evidence: Lines 180-185: readTable and readArray recursively call readFieldValue, which can parse nested tables (case 'F') and arrays (case 'A'). No recursion depth limit is enforced.

defects_to_look_for.mechanism: A length field read from untrusted input decides the size of a buffer, and that buffer is created before the corresponding payload has been shown to exist.
Decoding routines call one another in a cycle with nothing counting how deep the cycle has gone, so nesting in the input controls the depth.
